newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi says tough 1997 will take Italy into EMU.
newsitem.headline: Prodi says tough 1997 will take Italy into EMU.

text.p: Italy approved a no-nonsense budget on Friday in a headlong rush to sign up for a single European currency, but economists said they fear the measures could land the economy in full-blown recession.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi said after a 10-hour cabinet meeting that the heart of the budget would slice 36-37 trillion lire ($24 billion) from the public sector deficit.

An extra 13 trillion lire would be raised from a one-off "Eurotax" and a further 12 trillion would be squeezed from so-far-unspecified "treasury operations". Prodi said the budget would make sure Italy became a founder member of a European economic and monetary union (EMU) at its launch in 1999.
The cabinet would immediately reconvene to iron out final details of the draft budget law which parliament has to approve by the end of December, he added.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told the news conference two thirds of the budget would be made up of spending cuts with the balance coming from fresh revenues.
Economists said a hefty dose of new taxes could deal a body blow to an economy already struggling in the face of flat consumer demand and flagging exports.
The government says it is counting on the central bank to deliver a string of interest rate cuts that will reduce the cost of borrowing money in time to make up for the fiscal tightening.

"On the growth side, a package of this size will have dire consequences," said Sally Wilkinson, a London-based economist at Swiss bank UBS. "To impose a severe fiscal package at a time of slow growth and an appreciating currency would be suicide."

"It's clear the Eurotax would lower consumption and with the economy already practically in recession the situation could become dangerous," said another economist at an international investment bank in London who asked not to be named.

Italian bond markets and the lira have soared in recent days on a tidal wave of optimism over Italy's chances of meeting strict qualifying criteria for membership of European economic and monetary union (EMU) by 1999.

Diego Masi, the parliamentary leader of Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini's centrist Italian Renewal party, resigned in protest on Friday saying the government had caved in to pressure from hard-left leader Fausto Bertinotti.

Prodi has quietly shelved plans to tax pensions and raise charges for hospital treatment after Bertinotti threatened to scupper the budget in parliament. The centre-left government relies on support from Bertinotti's Marxist-inspired Communist Refoundation in the lower house.

The planned budget is far in excess of the 32.4 trillion lire the government originally intended to shave from the public sector deficit and aims to cut Italy's deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio to three percent by the end of next year.
Achievement of the three percent deficit target would put Italy on course to join an advance party of countries establishing a single European currency in 1999.
If the budget were to accelerate the slowdown, Italy would face falling tax revenues making it harder to close a deficit which is heading for six percent at the end of this year.
Ciampi said in a front-page article in Friday's Corriere della Sera daily that Italy had to deliver a credible budget if it wanted to secure a lasting fall in interest rates.
"We have a duty to generate credibility. It is the path to reduce interest rates and therefore the deficit," Ciampi said. $1= 1,520 lire
